title: Predicting evolutionary rate as a pretraining task improves genome language model representations
claim: Composable pretraining targets (sequence, evolutionary rate, or both) under masked or autoregressive objectives yield genome-scale predictions that track biological conservation.
layout: 3 panels: genome-browser top, 3x2 objective grid bottom-left, model schematic right
description: Panel A is a genome-browser screenshot (chr6 p21.33). It stacks tracks for RefSeq genes, ENCODE cCREs, H3K27Ac, and basewise PhyloP conservation. At the bottom, a large blue track of model-predicted PhyloP follows the conservation peaks. Panel B is a 3x2 grid of nucleotide-strip diagrams. The columns are Sequence only, Evolutionary-rate only, and Sequence + evolutionary-rate. The rows are bi-directional (masked token) and uni-directional (next token). Colored A/T/G/C boxes sit beside teal-to-pink numeric rate strips. Each cell has an arrow, a formula such as f(x1..xn)=p(x̂i), and a highlighted predicted token. Panel C, at the right, shows genomic element annotations (promoter, exon, UCNE, enhancer, repeat) feeding stacked-layer model blocks. These lead to a 3D embedding axis plot and an ATG start-codon example.

abstract: Genome language models (gLM) have the potential to further understanding of regulatory genomics without requiring labeled data. Most gLMs are pretrained using sequence reconstruction tasks inspired by natural language processing, but recent studies have shown that these gLMs often fail to capture biological signal. To overcome this, we introduce pretraining tasks that predict the rate of evolution. These tasks are designed so that they can be composed with sequence reconstruction, enabling a controlled comparison of predicting sequence only, evolutionary rate only, or both. To address gaps in existing evaluations, we developed a suite of biologically grounded benchmarks. Across these tasks, and for established variant effect prediction benchmarks, models pretrained on both sequence and evolutionary rate outperform those trained on sequence alone, and training on evolutionary rate can make the even the relatively small models in our work competitive with much larger existing gLMs for some tasks on the human genome. These results establish evolution as a key training target for genome-scale models.
